title: Agentic Evaluations at Scale, For Everybody — Nicholas Kang & Michael Aaron, Google DeepMind

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about measuring AI systems through benchmarks, agent exams, PvP game arenas, and open eval platforms, making evaluation methodology the central subject. Kaggle's community eval infrastructure targets all AI practitioners and is not tied to any single application vertical. The talk focuses exclusively on the evaluation and benchmarking stage of the AI lifecycle. The presentation blends accessible problem framing with technical details like Bradley-Terry scheduling and Elo ratings, fitting an intermediate level. This is a recorded conference presentation delivered by two speakers at Google DeepMind. Seven evidence anchors directly support evaluation as the primary focus, covering benchmark staleness, transparency, agent exams, Game Arena, and harness ambiguity.

summary: Nicholas Kang and Michael Aaron from Google DeepMind's Kaggle team argue that AI evaluations are fundamentally broken and propose community-driven infrastructure to fix them. Three problems are identified: (1) evals are scattered, decentralized, and go stale quickly, with 10+ benchmarks published daily and leaderboards abandoned; (2) evals lack transparency, as model publishers may optimize configurations like compaction without disclosure, producing misleading results; (3) evals are created by a tiny population of ~30,000 AI researchers while ~30 million technical professionals exist, meaning domain expertise from fields like wastewater treatment is never captured. Four solutions are presented. Hackathons channel community energy with guardrails; a current hackathon with Google DeepMind's AGI team focuses on five of ten cognitive faculties. Standardized agent exams let users paste a one-line prompt to test their agent and receive a leaderboard score; the MVP launched the prior week and drew 500+ agent evaluations without promotion, with spin-off community posts and an SAE prep course emerging. A PvP Game Arena provides evergreen, unsaturated Elo-based ratings through games like Werewolf (deception), poker (randomization and deception), and chess. Model personalities emerge: Grok goes all-in aggressively on poker while newer models are more risk-averse and perform worse. The arena runs on the Kaggle simulation platform using OpenSpiel games, an LLM model proxy, and Bradley-Terry pairwise scheduling to reduce the number of games needed. Major challenges include cost (400,000 poker hands were needed for statistical significance), keeping the experience engaging for the community, and comparing models over time as endpoints may not honestly report which model is serving. An open benchmark platform lets anyone build, run, and share evals with assertions and LLM judging, similar to production eval platforms but community-focused. An example task by Paige involved parsing and recreating an SVG from XKCD. Benchmark challenges include incentivizing community contributions, agentic benchmark ambiguity (a Morph LLM blog post noted six frontier models on SWE-Bench Pro are within a couple percentage points, but harness choice shifts performance by 22%), and fast model release and deprecation cycles complicating longitudinal comparisons.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Introductions
sections.summary: Nicholas Kang introduces himself as a PM in Kaggle Benchmarks running the platform and agentic eval solutions, based in SF Bay Area, originally from Singapore. Michael Aaron introduces himself as a software engineer at Google for about a third of his life, at Kaggle for half of that, currently focused on evaluations and benchmarks.

sections.title: Kaggle Overview and Agenda
sections.summary: Kaggle is the world's largest AI/ML community with 30+ million users, known for competitions but increasingly working in GenAI Eval. The agenda covers why AI evals are broken today and what Kaggle is doing to solve it, including challenges and invitation for community contributions.

sections.title: Problem 1: Evals Are Scattered, Decentralized, and Stale
sections.summary: 10+ benchmarks drop daily, best discovered by scrolling arxiv for hours. After publication, leaderboards go stale as authors move to the next benchmark. Even as a full-time job, Nick cannot keep up.

sections.title: Problem 2: Evals Aren't Transparent, Accessible, or Verifiable
sections.summary: Model publisher charts don't reveal benchmark setup or model configurations. A competing AI lab reran a Kaggle-published benchmark using their own compaction settings via their API, producing much better results. Neither result was wrong but the difference was undisclosed.

sections.title: Problem 3: Evals Created by a Tiny Fraction of People
sections.summary: ~30,000 AI researchers create evals while ~30 million technical professionals exist. Unevaluated capabilities lead to cognitive jaggedness. The wastewater treatment plant engineer from Turkey, with 20 years of experience, built a novel safety benchmark after incidents where protocol violations caused deaths. This proprietary dataset exists nowhere else and isn't economically productive for AI labs.

sections.title: Solutions Overview
sections.summary: Four solutions introduced: hackathons (channel community energy), standardized agent exams (democratize evals for consumer agents), Game Arena (PvP Elo-based evergreen benchmark), and the benchmark platform (anyone can build, run, share evals). Nick covers the first two; Michael deep dives into the latter two.

sections.title: Hackathons: Approach and Challenges
sections.summary: Hackathons channel energy and expertise with guardrails. Currently running one with Google DeepMind's AGI team on five of ten cognitive faculties from a recent paper. Challenges include: providing tools and API access to participants who can't afford model API keys, enabling shareable write-ups, and facilitating human expert judging since AI agents aren't good at evaluating innovation and creativity.

sections.title: Standardized Agent Exams
sections.summary: Originally called SATs (trademark issue forced rename). Users paste a one-line prompt and the agent takes an exam, returning a score on a leaderboard. MVP launched the prior week and drew 500+ agent evaluations without promotion. Spin-off community posts appeared on Mopbook, including an SAE prep course. Tension exists between making exams accessible and challenging enough; if too difficult no one finishes, if too easy the signal is weak.

sections.title: Game Arena: Overview and Games
sections.summary: Michael Aaron introduces Game Arena as a PvP benchmarking platform that avoids saturation since one model can always compete against another. Games are chosen to test varied capabilities: Werewolf for deception, poker for randomization and deception, and chess. Model personalities emerge: Grok loves to go all-in on poker while newer, more risk-averse models perform worse. The engineering process involves designing and iterating games, ensuring models can play them, and refining prompts for fairness. Everything is open source on GitHub.

sections.title: Game Arena: Infrastructure and Pipeline
sections.summary: The harness is built on OpenSpiel (an RL framework) and runs on the Kaggle simulation platform, originally an RL platform. An LLM model proxy on Colab provides consistent communication across models. Bradley-Terry pairwise scheduling reduces the number of games needed. Results are published as LLM conversation datasets on Kaggle, Elo scores on the benchmarks page, and a game visualizer lets users watch games like Grok going all-in on poker hands.

sections.title: Game Arena: Challenges
sections.summary: Major challenges include cost (400,000 poker hands were needed for statistical significance, with many turns per hand), repetitiveness making community engagement difficult, and comparing models over time as old models disappear, new models arrive, and endpoints may not honestly report which model is serving. Ideas for engagement include community-contributed prompts for hackathons where users compete to prompt models best.

sections.title: Open Benchmark Platform
sections.summary: Not a production evaluation platform but a community-focused one where anyone can build, run, and share evals openly and verifiably. Architecture mirrors production platforms: assertions (e.g., does this contain a towel), LLM judging, tasks grouped and evaluated against user-selected models, aggregated into benchmarks. Example: Paige created a task parsing an SVG from XKCD with assertions checking whether the model can generate an SVG, produce correct text, and other checks, with side-by-side model comparison. Sonic 4 produced a nice reproduction.

sections.title: Benchmark Challenges and Closing
sections.summary: Challenges include incentivizing community benchmark creation (hackathons and Kaggle's points/medal system help, but writing good evaluations takes significant work). Agentic benchmark execution is hard: a Morph LLM blog post noted that on SWE-Bench Pro, six frontier models are within a couple percentage points, but harness choice creates a 22% difference, creating ambiguity about whether the model or harness is being tested. Fast model release and deprecation cycles further complicate longitudinal comparison. Michael and Nick invite attendees to find them at the DeepMind booth or email them.
